source_text: Verumtamen procudere disputationem de necessariis fidei non est otiosum, quia nec infructuosum. loquacitas in aedificatione nulla turpis, si quando turpis. itaque si de aliquo bono sermo est, res postulat contrarium quoque boni recensere. quid enim sectandum sit, magis inluminabis, si, quid uitandum sit, proinde digesseris. consideremus igitur de impatientia, an sicut patientia in deo, ita aduersaria eius in aduersario nostro nata atque comperta sit, ut ex isto appareat, quam principaliter fidei aduersetur. nam quod ab aemulo dei conceptum est utique non est amicum dei rebus. eadem discordia est rerum quae et auctorum. porro cum deus optimus, diabolus e contrario pessimus, ipsa sui diuersitate testantur neutrum alterius facere, ut nobis non magis a malo aliquid boni quam a bono aliquid mali editum uideri possit. igitur natales impatientiae in ipso diabolo deprehendo, iam tunc, cum dominum deum uniuersa opera, quae fecisset, imagini suae, id est homini, subiecisse impatienter tulit nec enim doluisset, si sustinuisset, -nec inuidisset homini, si non doluisset. adeo decepit eum, quia inuiderat; inuiderat autem, quia doluerat; doluerat (autem,) quia patienter utique non tulerat. quid prius fuerit ille angelus perditionis, malus an impatiens, contemno quaerere, palam cum sit aut impatientiam ab malitia aut malitiam ab impatientia auspicatam deinde inter se conspirasse et indiuiduas in uno patris sinu adoleuisse. at enim quam prius senserat, per quam [primus] delinquere intrauerat, de suo experimento quid ad peccandum adiutaret (in)structus, eandem impingendo in crimen homini aduocauit. conuenta statim illi mulier, non temere dixerim, per conloquium ipsum eius afflata est spiritu impatientia infecto. usque adeo numquam omnino peccasset, si diuino interdicto patientiam perseruasset. quid, quod non sustinuit sola conuenta, sed apud Adam, nondum maritum, nondum aures sibi debentem, impatiens etiam tacendi est ac traducem illum eius, quod a malo hauserat, facit? perit igitur et alius homo per impatientiam alterius, perit(urus) mox et ipse per impatientiam suam utrobique commissam et circa dei praemonitionem et circa diaboli circumscriptionem, illam seruare, hanc refutare non sustinens. hinc prima iudicii, unde delicti, origo; hinc deus irasci exorsus, unde offendere homo inductus. [inde in deo prima patientia, unde indignatio prima, qui tunc maledictione sola contentus ab animaduersionis impetu in diabolo temptatoris] aut quod crimen ante istud impatientiae admissum homini imputatur? innocens erat et deo de proximo amicus et paradisi colonus. at ubi semel succidit impatientiae, desiuit deo sapere, desiuit caelestia sustinere posse, exinde homo, terrae datus et ab oculis dei eiectus, facile usurpari ab impatientia coepit in omne, quod deum offenderet. nam statim illa semine diaboli concepta malitiae fecunditate iram filium procreauit, editum suis artibus erudiit. quod enim ipsa Adam et Euam morti inmerserat, docuit et filium ab homicidio incipere. frustra istud impatientiae adscripserim, si Cain ille primus homicida et primus fratricida oblationes suas a domino recusatas aequanimiter nec impatienter tulit, si iratus fratri suo non est, si neminem denique interemit. cum uero nec occidere potuerit nisi iratus nec irasci nisi impatiens, demonstrat quod per iram gessit ad eam referendum, a qua ira suggesta est. [per] haec impatientiae tunc infantis quodammodo incunabula. ceterum quanta mox incrementa! nec mirum. nam si prima deliquit, consequens est, at, quia prima, idcirco et sola sit matrix in omne delictum, + defundens de suo fonte uarias criminum uenas. de homicidio quidem dictum est. sed ira editum a primordio, etiam quascumque postmodum causas sibi inuenit ad impatientiam at ad originem sui confert. sine enim quis inimicitiis siue praedae gratia id scelus conficit, prius est, ut aut odii aut auaritiae fiat impatiens. quidquid compellit, sine impatientia scelus non est ut perfici possit. quis adulterium sine libidinis impatientia subiit? quod et si pretio in feminis cogitur., uenditio illa pudicitiae utique impatientia contemnendi lucri ordinatur. haec ut principalia penes dominum delicta. nam ut compendio dictum sit, omne peccatum impatientiae adscribendum. malum impatientia est boni. nemo impudicus non impatiens pudicitiae et improbus probitatis et impius pietatis et inquietus quietis. ut malus unusquisque fiat, bonus perseuerare non poterit. talis igitur excetra delictorum cur non dominum offendat improbatorem malorum? an non ipsum quoque Israhel per impatientiam semper in deum deliquisse manifestum est, exinde, cum oblitus brachii caelestis, quo Aegyptiis adflictationibus fuerat extractus, de Aaron deos sibi duces postulat, cum in idolum auri sui conlationes defundit? tam necessarias enim Moysei cum domino congredientis impatienter exceperat moras. post mannae escatilem pluuiam, post petrae aquatilem sequellam desperant de domino, tridui sitim non sustinendo. nam haec quoque illis impatientia a domino exprobratur. ac ne singula peruagemur: numquam non per impatientiam delinquendo (per impatientiam) perierunt. quomodo autem manus prophetis intulerunt, nisi per impatientiam audiendi? domino autem ipso, per impatientiam etiam uidendi. quodsi patientiam inissent,\' liberarentur.
thought_title: Impatience originates with the devil and is the root of every sin
orientation: Tertullian has just opened the treatise by saying that discussing the things necessary to faith is useful, and now he begins his argument by tracing impatience to its origin in the devil.
pass_a_gloss: But to hammer out a discussion about the things necessary to faith is not idle, because it is not unfruitful either. Talkativeness in building up is never shameful, if ever it is shameful. And so if the talk is about some good thing, the matter demands that the opposite of the good also be reviewed. For you will illuminate more what should be pursued, if you have likewise set out what should be avoided. Let us consider therefore about impatience, whether just as patience is in God, so its adversary was born and discovered in our adversary, so that from this it may appear how principally it opposes faith. For what was conceived by the rival of God is certainly not friendly to the things of God. The discord of the things is the same as that of their authors. Furthermore, since God is best, the devil on the contrary worst, by their very difference they testify that neither does the work of the other, so that to us nothing good can seem to have been produced from the evil one any more than anything evil from the good one. Therefore I detect the birth of impatience in the devil himself, already then, when he impatiently bore it that the Lord God had subjected all the works which he had made to his image, that is, to man. For he would not have grieved, if he had endured it, and he would not have envied man, if he had not grieved. So much did it deceive him, because he had envied; but he had envied, because he had grieved; but he had grieved, because he had certainly not borne it patiently. What that angel of perdition was first, evil or impatient, I decline to ask, since it is plain that either impatience began from malice or malice from impatience, and that they then conspired together and grew up inseparable in the bosom of one father. But indeed the very thing which he had first felt, through which he had first entered into sinning, instructed by his own experience as to what would help toward sinning, he summoned against man by driving the same thing into crime. The woman was at once approached by him; I would not rashly say that she was breathed upon by his spirit infected with impatience through the conversation itself. To such a degree she would never have sinned at all, if she had preserved patience toward the divine prohibition. What of the fact that she did not endure being approached alone, but in the presence of Adam, not yet her husband, not yet owing his ears to her, she is impatient even of keeping silent and makes him a conduit of that which she had drawn from the evil one? Therefore another man also perishes through the impatience of another, and he himself is soon going to perish through his own impatience, committed in both directions, both concerning God's forewarning and concerning the devil's deception, not enduring to keep the former and to refuse the latter. From here is the first origin of judgment, from where the origin of the offense was; from here God began to be angry, from where man was led to offend. Then in God was the first patience, from where the first indignation was, who then, content with a curse alone, refrained from the assault of punishment upon the devil the tempter. Or what crime before this crime of impatience is charged to man? He was innocent and recently a friend of God and a cultivator of paradise. But once he fell under impatience, he ceased to be wise toward God, he ceased to be able to endure heavenly things. From then on man, given to the earth and cast out from the eyes of God, began easily to be taken over by impatience into everything that would offend God. For immediately that impatience, conceived by the seed of the devil with the fertility of malice, brought forth anger as a son, and trained the offspring in its own arts. For what it had plunged Adam and Eve into, death, it taught the son also to begin from homicide. I would ascribe this to impatience in vain, if that Cain, the first murderer and first fratricide, bore his offerings refused by the Lord calmly and not impatiently, if he was not angry with his brother, if he killed no one at all. But since he could not have killed unless angry, nor been angry unless impatient, it shows that what he did through anger must be referred to that from which anger was suggested. These are the cradles, so to speak, of impatience then in its infancy. But how great its growths soon were! And no wonder. For if it sinned first, it follows that, because it is first, for that reason it is also the sole womb of every offense, pouring out from its own source various veins of crimes. About homicide indeed it has been said. But since anger was brought forth by it from the beginning, whatever causes it afterward found for itself for impatience, it refers them to its own origin. For whether someone accomplishes that crime for the sake of enmities or for the sake of plunder, it comes first that he becomes impatient either of hatred or of greed. Whatever compels, without impatience a crime cannot be accomplished. Who has undergone adultery without impatience of lust? And even if it is forced upon women by a price, that sale of chastity is certainly arranged by impatience of despising gain. These are the principal offenses in the sight of the Lord. For to say it briefly, every sin must be ascribed to impatience. Impatience is the evil of good. No one is unchaste without being impatient of chastity, nor wicked without being impatient of uprightness, nor impious without being impatient of piety, nor restless without being impatient of quiet. In order for anyone to become evil, he will not be able to persevere in being good. Therefore such a hydra of offenses, why should it not offend the Lord, the disapprover of evils? Or is it not also manifest that Israel itself always sinned against God through impatience, from the time when, forgetting the heavenly arm by which it had been drawn out from the afflictions of the Egyptians, it demanded gods from Aaron as leaders for itself, when it poured out contributions of its gold into an idol? For it had impatiently endured the delays of Moses, so necessary, while he was meeting with the Lord. After the edible rain of manna, after the watery following of the rock, they despair of the Lord, not enduring a three-day thirst. For this impatience too is reproached to them by the Lord. And not to wander through individual cases: never did they perish except by sinning through impatience. But how did they lay hands on the prophets, except through impatience of hearing? And on the Lord himself, through impatience even of seeing. But if they had entered into patience, they would have been freed.

choices.why: The verb procudere means literally to forge or hammer out metal; keeping the metaphor preserves Tertullian's vivid image of intellectual labor.
The brief identifies the devil as 'aemulus dei'; 'rival' captures the competitive hostility better than 'enemy' here.

choices.term: traducem illum eius, quod a malo hauserat, facit
choices.english: makes him a conduit of that which she had drawn from the evil one
choices.why: Tradux literally means a vine-layer or channel; 'conduit' preserves the image of transmission from the devil through Eve to Adam.

choices.english: the sole womb of every offense
choices.why: Matrix is literally 'womb'; keeping the bodily image matches Tertullian's metaphor of impatience giving birth to sins.
rejected: the sole source of every sin

choices.why: Excetra is a water-serpent or hydra; the mythological monster whose heads multiply fits Tertullian's point that impatience spawns endless sins.
Escatilis is a rare adjective from esca, 'food'; 'edible rain' renders the oddity of the Latin rather than normalizing it to 'manna'.

bible_refs.note: The devil's approach to Eve and her conversation with him, leading to the fall.
Cain's offering refused and his murder of Abel.
Israel demanding gods from Aaron and making the golden calf while Moses delayed.
Israel's complaint about food in the wilderness, the manna.
Israel's thirst at Rephidim and the water from the rock.

pass_b_english: But to hammer out a discussion of matters essential to faith is not idle, because it is not fruitless either. Talk that builds up is never shameful, if it is ever shameful at all. So when the subject is some good thing, the case demands that we also review its opposite. For you will throw more light on what should be pursued if you likewise set out what should be avoided. Let us consider, then, whether impatience, just as patience is in God, was likewise born and discovered in our adversary, so that from this it may appear how fundamentally it opposes faith. For what was conceived by the rival of God is certainly no friend to the things of God. The same discord exists between the things as between their authors. Moreover, since God is the best and the devil by contrast the worst, their very difference testifies that neither does the work of the other, so that we cannot think that anything good has been produced by the evil one any more than anything evil by the good one.

I detect the birth of impatience in the devil himself, already at that time when he impatiently bore the Lord God subjecting all the works he had made to his own image, that is, to man. For he would not have grieved if he had endured it, and he would not have envied man if he had not grieved. He deceived him because he had envied; he had envied because he had grieved; he had grieved because he had certainly not borne it patiently. Whether that angel of perdition was evil or impatient first, I do not care to ask, since it is plain that either impatience began from malice or malice from impatience, and that they then conspired together and grew up inseparable in the bosom of one father. But the very thing he had first experienced, through which he had entered into sin, he knew from his own trial what would help toward sinning, and he summoned it to drive man into crime. The woman, met by him at once, and I would not rashly say that through that very conversation she was breathed upon by his spirit, infected with impatience. So much so that she would never have sinned at all if she had preserved patience toward the divine prohibition. What of the fact that she alone did not endure being approached, but with Adam—not yet her husband, not yet owing her his ears—she was impatient even of silence, and made him a conduit of that which she had drawn from the evil one? So another man also perishes through the impatience of another, and he himself would soon perish through his own impatience, committed in both directions: toward God's warning and toward the devil's deception, not enduring to keep the former and refuse the latter. From here came the first origin of judgment, as of the offense; from here God began to be angry, where man was led to offend. From then on God's first patience, whence his first indignation; he who was then content with a curse alone held back from the impulse of punishment against the devil the tempter. Or what crime committed before this impatience is charged to man? He was innocent, a friend of God in close proximity, and a cultivator of paradise. But once he fell under impatience, he ceased to have a taste for God, ceased to be able to endure heavenly things. From then on man, given to the earth and cast out from God's eyes, began easily to be seized by impatience in everything that would offend God.

For immediately that impatience, conceived by the seed of the devil with the fertility of malice, gave birth to a son, wrath, and trained the offspring in her own arts. For what she herself had plunged Adam and Eve into—death—she also taught her son to begin with homicide. I would ascribe this to impatience in vain, if that Cain, the first murderer and first fratricide, bore his offerings being refused by the Lord calmly and not impatiently; if he was not angry with his brother; if, in short, he killed no one. But since he could not have killed unless angry, nor been angry unless impatient, it shows that what he did through anger must be referred to that from which anger was suggested. These were the cradles, so to speak, of impatience in its infancy. But how great its growth soon after! And no wonder. For if it sinned first, it follows that, because it was first, it is also the sole womb of every offense, pouring from its own fountain the varied streams of crimes. Homicide has indeed been mentioned. But since wrath was born from the beginning, whatever causes it afterward found for itself, it refers to impatience as to its own origin. For whether someone commits that crime out of enmity or for plunder, the first thing is that he becomes impatient either of hatred or of greed. Whatever compels him, without impatience no crime can be accomplished. Who has entered into adultery without impatience of lust? And if it is forced upon women by payment, that sale of chastity is certainly arranged by impatience of scorning gain. These are the principal offenses in the Lord's sight. For to put it briefly, every sin must be ascribed to impatience. Impatience is the evil of good. No one is unchaste without being impatient of chastity, nor dishonest without impatience of honesty, nor impious without impatience of piety, nor restless without impatience of quiet. For anyone to become evil, he cannot persevere in being good.

Such a hydra of offenses, then—why would it not offend the Lord, who disapproves of evils? Is it not also manifest that Israel itself always sinned against God through impatience, from the time when, forgetting the heavenly arm by which it had been drawn out from the afflictions of Egypt, it demanded gods from Aaron to lead it, and poured its contributions into an idol of its gold? For Moses, when meeting with the Lord, impatiently received the necessary delays. After the edible rain of manna, after the watery stream from the rock, they despaired of the Lord, not enduring a three-day thirst. For this too is charged against them by the Lord as impatience. And not to wander through every instance: they never sinned except through impatience, and through impatience they perished. How did they lay hands on the prophets, except through impatience of hearing? And on the Lord himself, through impatience even of seeing. But if they had entered into patience, they would have been set free.
notes: The text contains a bracketed passage '[inde in deo prima patientia, unde indignatio prima, qui tunc maledictione sola contentus ab animaduersionis impetu in diabolo temptatoris]' which appears to be a marginal gloss or later insertion; it is translated as part of the running text but is syntactically awkward.

The phrase '+ defundens de suo fonte uarias criminum uenas' is marked with a crux in the source, indicating textual uncertainty; the gloss renders it as 'pouring out from its own source various veins of crimes'.

problems.quote: she did not endure being approached alone
problems.why: sola is feminine nominative: Eve alone did not endure; not that she didn't endure being approached alone.
problems.fix: she alone did not endure being approached
problems.ruling: Latin 'sola conuenta' = 'the woman alone', not 'being approached alone'; English adds wrong circumstance.

problems.quote: From then on God's first patience, where his first indignation, who then, content with a curse alone, held back from the force of punishment against the devil the tempter.
problems.source_quote: inde in deo prima patientia, unde indignatio prima, qui tunc maledictione sola contentus ab animaduersionis impetu in diabolo temptatoris
problems.why: Garbled: source says God's first patience began where his first indignation did—yet he then, content with curse alone, refrained from punishment against the devil.
problems.fix: From then on God's first patience, whence his first indignation; yet he then, content with a curse alone, held back from the force of punishment against the devil the tempter.
problems.ruling: Latin 'prima patientia, unde indignatio prima, qui tunc maledictione sola contentus...' differs from garbled English about God holding back punishment.

problems.quote: it had impatiently endured the delays of Moses, necessary as they were, while he was meeting with God
problems.source_quote: tam necessarias enim Moysei cum domino congredientis impatienter exceperat moras
problems.why: Latin says Moses impatiently received the delays; English reverses agency, making Israel the impatient party.
problems.fix: Moses, when meeting with the Lord, impatiently received the necessary delays.
problems.ruling: Latin 'Moysei...exceperat moras' means Moses impatiently endured delays; English wrongly attributes impatience to Israel instead.

fixed: Confirmed: 'illam seruare, hanc refutare non sustinens' — 'illam' refers to God's warning (keep), 'hanc' to the devil's deception (refuse). The English 'the one...the other' is ambiguous and reverses the antecedents; changed to 'the former...the latter' to match the source order.

dismissed.quote: he impatiently bore the Lord God subjecting all the works he had made to his own image, that is, to man
dismissed.why: Latin says the devil subjects the Lord God (or works) to man's image; English makes the Lord God the subject of subjection, reversing agency.
dismissed.note: This is an accusative-plus-infinitive: the devil 'impatiently bore that the Lord God had subjected' his works to man, which the English renders correctly.
